newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN mandate for U.S. attacks ambiguous.
newsitem.headline: UN mandate for U.S. attacks ambiguous.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday used a 1991 Security Council resolution to justify its missile attack on southern Iraq but it was questionable if the resolution in fact mandated such action.
The Security Council meets late on Tuesday to discuss Iraq's offensive in the northern Kurdish areas, with some Western envoys wanting a condemnation of the Iraqi action.
But so far the United States has received open support only from Britain and Germany, both council members, for its early morning cruise missile attack against Iraqi installations.

China and Russia have urged restraint and France, throughout the past week, has been cautious, expressing concern about President Saddam Hussein's march into Kurdish-dominated provinces in the north but also saying the territorial integrity of Iraq needs to be observed. Developing nations on the council are expected to be reserved also.
The United States, Britain, France, China and Russia are permanent members of the 15-seat council.

Washington for several years has invoked U.N. Security Council Resolution 688, adopted on April 5, 1991, to condemn the Iraqi government's repression of minorities, as an underpinning for military action and creating no-fly zones in the northern and the southern parts of the country.

It was adopted when Kurds in the north and Shiites in the south rose up against Saddam Hussein's government in the spring of 1991 after the Gulf War. The Kurds fled to Turkey and Iran, pursued by Iraqi troops and strafed from the air, prompting a worldwide outcry.

Resolution 688, while encouraging widespread relief aid to the Kurds by international organisations after the Gulf War, did not specifically set up a safe haven off limits to Iraqi troops and deliberately excluded the use of military force.

China had threatened to veto any measure that would justify foreign military intervention in Iraq during the 1991 debate on the resolution which was initiated by France's late president, Francois Mitterrand.

In subsequent years, the United States, Britain and France kept their dealings with Iraq on the no-fly zones away from the Security Council, thereby giving credence to those who maintained the West was stretching the interpretation of Resolution 688.

But council members turned a blind eye to the exclusionary zone in the north, with many states believing that allied protection was necessary to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe that followed the Gulf War, which the U.N. authorised. The then-Soviet Union also supported the zone.
Shortly afterwards the allies as well as U.N. humanitarian groups moved in to provide shelter for the Kurds and Iraq was warned not to fly any aircraft over the area.
In the summer of 1992, the allies cited the same resolution when they banned Iraq from flying over the southern marshes where Shiite rebels were hiding.
But even in early 1993 when U.S. President Bill Clinton launched a raid on Iraqi missile batteries in the south, the council made sure its statements ignored the bombing.
